title: Volume of Solids
status: draft: written 18 Nov 2026 offline for Grade 9; not yet checked by a Kenyan maths teacher; not loaded by the live tutor
notes: Official outcomes a to e are tested; f (promote the use) is not a question. Volume of triangular and rectangular prisms (a), pyramids as one third of the prism on the same base (b), cones (c), frustums as a big cone minus the small cone cut off (d) and spheres and hemispheres (e), with capacity in litres. Grade 7 did cuboids and cylinders. g9.vol.frustum-scale uses the cube of the scale factor for the cut-off cone, which links to Similarity and Enlargement; a teacher should confirm learners meet volume scale factors before this family.

skills.key_step: The child finds the area of the end first, multiplies by the length, then changes units in one separate step.

floor.prerequisite: Finds the volume of a cuboid.
floor.question: 2 by 3 by 4

representations: a units ladder cubic cm to litres
contexts: a school swimming pool with a sloping floor
a water tank on a stand

board.do: Draw a trough with a triangular end and slices along its length.

board.say: How much water is in one 1 cm slice?

board.do: Wait for the area of the end.

misconceptions.ask: Is the end a rectangle?
Is a cubic cm a litre?
Does the trough come to a point?
How many cubic cm in a litre?
Area of a trapezium?
misconceptions.repair: Half the sum times the length.

misconceptions.ask: Is that the wall or the water?
Slices: add or multiply?
Did the wall already use the 20 m?
Is a cubic metre bigger than a litre?

checks.question: A prism has triangular ends of base 20 cm and height 15 cm, and is 80 cm long. Litres?
A pool 8 m wide, depths 1 m and 2 m, 25 m long. Volume?

skills.key_step: The child writes one third of base area times height, and to work back multiplies the volume by 3 before dividing by the base area.

floor.prerequisite: Finds the volume of a prism.
floor.question: Base 36, height 4

steps: To work back: 3 x volume / base area.
contexts: a sand mould at the beach

board.do: Draw a pyramid inside a cuboid with the same base and height.

board.say: How many pyramids of water fill it?

board.do: Write three: the pyramid is one third.

misconceptions.ask: How many pyramids fill the cuboid?
Does the pyramid fill the corners?
Is the pyramid bigger?
Is 20 the pyramid or the empty space?
Where is the third?
Is 6 the area of the base?
Is the monument taller than its volume?
misconceptions.repair: No: divide by the base area.

misconceptions.ask: How do you undo taking one third?

checks.question: A pyramid has a square base of side 9 m and height 10 m. Volume?
A pyramid of volume 80 cubic cm has a base of 4 cm by 6 cm. Height?

skills.key_step: The child writes one third pi r squared h with the radius, then uses the volume for the question asked (trips, litres) and rounds by the story.

floor.prerequisite: Finds the volume of a cylinder.
floor.question: r = 7, h = 10

representations: one third pi r squared h
steps: Use it: divide by a load, change to litres.
contexts: a heap of sand at a building site
a heap of maize at a store

board.do: Draw a cone inside a cylinder with the same base and height.
Write volume = 1/3 pi r squared h.

misconceptions.ask: Is the heap a cylinder?
Is 7 the radius?
Were trips asked?
Did the question give the diameter?
Is all the sand moved after 4 trips?

checks.question: A cone has radius 6 cm and height 14 cm. Volume? (pi = 22/7)
A heap of 40 cubic m of sand; a lorry carries 7 cubic m. Trips?

skills.key_step: The child draws the whole cone and the small cone, labels each with its own radius and height, and subtracts.

floor.prerequisite: Finds the volume of a cone.
floor.question: r = 7, h = 15

representations: a bucket with the missing tip drawn in
a table of radius and height for each
steps: Volume of the small cone cut off.

board.do: Draw a bucket and dash in the missing tip to make a whole cone.

board.say: Is this part of the bucket?

board.do: Write bucket = big cone - small cone.

misconceptions.ask: Is a cone a cylinder?
Which radius belongs to the big cone?
How tall is the cut-off piece?
Is the tip part of the bucket?
Did you cut off the tip?
Every length halves. What happens to volume?
Is 1/4 for area or volume?
Which part holds the water?

checks.question: A whole cone holds 8,000 cubic cm. The tip cut off is half as tall. The frustum holds?
Big cone 4,312 cubic cm, small cone 539 cubic cm. Bucket in litres?

skills.key_step: The child writes the radius three times, uses four thirds for a sphere and two thirds for a hemisphere, and compares spheres by the cube of the radius.
representations: a table of radius and volume
steps: Sphere: times 4/3 pi. Hemisphere: times 2/3 pi.
For recasting: big volume / small volume.
contexts: melting metal balls at a jua kali workshop

board.say: The radius halves. What happens to the volume?

misconceptions.ask: Is the bowl a whole ball?
How many times is r used for volume?
Half of four thirds?
Is the bowl a cone?
Does the volume halve when the radius halves?
Is 4 for area or volume?
How many small ones fit the big one?
Is 6 three more than 3, or twice 3?
What is 3 cubed?

checks.question: Volume of a hemisphere of radius 3 cm in terms of pi?
A sphere of radius 4 cm is melted into spheres of radius 1 cm. How many?
